\chapter{He Hablado --- A Verb With No Meaning Left}
\label{ch:perfect-first-person}
\hlchaptermodality{95}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say he hablado, and say what haber contributes to it.}

Complete ES-C49-he-hablado: produce he hablado espanol and say what haber means there.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[he hablado]{he hablado — \textquotedblleft{}I have spoken\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C49-he-hablado}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{hablado}, and it cannot stand alone — it names no person and no time. It needs a word in front of it. Here is that word.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — the \emph{h} in \emph{he} is silent, as every Spanish \emph{h} is. It is one sound: \emph{eh}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the emptied verb}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{he} + participle — \emph{I have} done something.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{He hablado} español.} — I have spoken Spanish.
\end{quote}

Two words, and the work is split cleanly between them. \emph{He} carries the person and the tense. \emph{Hablado} carries the meaning. Neither does the other's job, and that division is why the participle never had to agree with anybody.

\emph{He} is a form of \textbf{haber} — and here is the thing worth the chapter: \textbf{haber does not mean anything here.} It is not \textquotedblleft{}I hold spoken.\textquotedblright{} You cannot translate it on its own. It is a word whose entire remaining purpose is to hold a participle in place.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Haber} comes from Latin \textbf{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold, to have\textquotedblright{} — a completely ordinary verb with a completely ordinary meaning.

Then Spanish did something drastic. It handed the \emph{meaning} to \textbf{tener} (which had been the narrower \textquotedblleft{}hold, grip\textquotedblright{}), and kept \emph{haber} for this one grammatical job. The verb was hollowed out: the meaning left, the machinery stayed.

\textbf{English did exactly the same thing to \emph{have}, and you never noticed.} When you say \emph{I have eaten}, nobody is holding anything. Two languages, independently, took their word for \textquotedblleft{}hold\textquotedblright{} and wore it down into a tense marker — because the step from \emph{I have a thing that is done} to \emph{I have done a thing} is a very short one, and everybody takes it eventually.

So when \emph{haber} feels meaningless, that is not a gap in your understanding. It is an accurate perception of what happened to the word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}He hablado español\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I have eaten\textquotedblright{} in English, and notice that nothing is being held
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I have spoken\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{He hablado}}.) Which word carries the meaning? (\emph{\textbf{Hablado}}.) And what does \emph{haber} contribute? (\textbf{A person and a tense} — and no meaning at all.) Next: the rest of it.
